title: Chapter 37 — 'I Need to Think About It'
intro: The vaguest objection on the floor — and the sorting question that turns it into something you can actually solve.

sections.title: What They Are Really Saying
sections.content:
'I need to think about it' is not an objection. It is a shield. Behind it could be anything: price concerns, spouse approval, fear of making the wrong choice, feeling overwhelmed, wanting to compare elsewhere, or simply not being asked directly enough.

The worst response is to say 'okay, take your time' and watch them leave. The best response is to gently find out what is actually behind the hesitation.

sections.title: The Sorting Question
sections.content:
Use one simple question to sort what is really going on: 'Of course — it is a big decision. If you don't mind me asking, is it the product itself you want to think about, or is it more about the timing or the investment?'

That question gives them three lanes: product, timing, or price. Whichever they choose tells you exactly where to focus.

If it is the product — you may need to revisit discovery. Maybe you recommended the wrong model.
If it is timing — explore what would make the timing right. Is there a deadline?
If it is price — address the value, financing, or find an alternative.

sections.title: The Structured Think
sections.content:
Sometimes the customer genuinely needs time. That is fine. But do not let them leave without structure.

Review what they liked. Confirm what worked. Identify what they are still unsure about. Then set a follow-up time.

'It sounds like the product is right but you want to sleep on the investment. That makes total sense. Would it be okay if I called you tomorrow afternoon to see where you landed?'

That is professional. It respects their process while keeping the sale alive.

sections.title: Coaching Rule
sections.content:
When evaluating this objection, ask:

Does the salesperson accept 'I need to think about it' at face value — or do they ask what specifically needs thinking about?
Can they sort the real concern — product, timing, or price?
Do they provide a structured follow-up plan — or just hope the customer returns?
Do they stay confident and professional — or appear desperate?

This objection is only vague if you let it stay vague.
